text: A fourteen-year-old has wired an old caravan into a radio station, and the voice he waits for belongs to his father, at work on a ship on the other side of the world. Then something crosses the signal: what sounds like a Latin mass. A school lesson on radio-astronomy supplies the rest, since waves a thousand years old are still arriving, and a boy who can solder hears that as a question of wire and height. Åke Sandgren gives it eighty minutes and the rhythm of children who have decided something and do not intend to be talked out of it: Sven, Bo and Petra, an aerial, an afternoon that gets away from them. The dialogue is Danish, the production Swedish, and the Guldbagge for Best Film went to a picture whose chief special effect is a caravan.

A widower, a housewife with empty afternoons, a gay lawyer: three people who never sit down together, and each gets a third of a film that runs a hundred and forty minutes. Ryosuke Hashiguchi keeps the strands apart. Nothing is arranged so that one life comments neatly on another, which leaves the rhymes to be felt rather than pointed at, and leaves the film a great deal of time to fill. It fills it with ordinary hours: errands, waiting, conversations that go around twice before anyone says the thing. Three different weights, carried at the same speed. Loss is the only thing the three share, and the film declines to treat that as a coincidence. Kinema Junpo named it the best film of its year, a strange fate for something built out of people not meeting.

Naniwa University Hospital, in Osaka, has two assistant professors who were classmates once and a ladder above them with fewer rungs than climbers. Goro Zaizen is the better surgeon and has organized his life around making sure the right people know it. Shuji Satomi stays with his patients and his research, which inside an institution like this is also a position, whether he intends it as one or not. Satsuo Yamamoto spends a hundred and fifty minutes here, and the length is not padding: promotions are made of meetings, and meetings take time. What the camera follows is less medicine than the arrangement of chairs around medicine, who is owed a favor, who signs, whose name is read out first. Both men are good at the work. Only one of them treats the hospital itself as the thing to be operated on.

The older detective's corruption is not a secret he keeps; it is a method, and he fully intends to pass it on. The younger one arrives with principles and a correction plan of his own, so the partnership turns into a contest over which man converts the other first, conducted at the volume of farce. The Baeksang for Best Film went to it, which is worth a moment, since nothing about a broad comedy on policemen who take money asks to be treated as the picture of the year. Then a case turns up that neither can work alone, and it is a strange one. Kang Woo-suk lets the comedy carry the weight and brings the action in when the plot needs somewhere to go, which is a fair description of how the two men operate as well.

He is dismissed from officer training for behaving strangely, and the next thing he does is stand in front of a biology class. At work they think he is deranged. At home a mother and a fiancee hold between them a complete account of what he ought to be doing with his life, so he takes a rented room and moves into it, roughly the amount of freedom a temporary teacher could afford in Sweden in 1974. Jan Halldoff then does the uncomfortable thing and lets the man start circling one of his own students. The film neither excuses this nor works it up into a case history. It stays at the eye level of someone managed by other people since childhood, who has just worked out that decisions are available to him and has never been told which ones are his to make.

Someone is setting fires across Seoul, and the men on the trail are fire investigators, which puts the chase inside the burning building rather than out on the road. Yang Yun-ho takes that difference seriously. The case has to be assembled from what fire leaves behind, by the same crew that will be sent into the smoke when the next call comes, so the deduction and the danger land on one set of shoulders. It changes what nerve looks like on screen: not a drawn weapon but a decision to go up one more floor. Two hours is a long time to keep a city burning, and Yang uses the length to make the arsonist a problem of evidence and a problem of physics at once. The film is candid about which of the two is harder to sit with.

Eighty-nine minutes is not much room for what this film is carrying: a wife dying of cancer, and a young woman at the office the husband cannot stop picturing. Im Kwon-taek puts both inside the same working week. The hospital and the desk belong to the same seven days, the same phone, the same tired man doing everything correctly and finding his attention going where he would rather it did not. Nothing here flatters him. The film declines to call the drift a betrayal and declines to file it under mourning, and it holds still long enough for the grief and the wanting to look like one condition rather than two, which is the harder and less comfortable claim. What is left is small, plain, and unusually exact about hours that nobody describes afterward.

A schoolteacher is posted by the government to a hamlet in Jujuy, in the northwest of Argentina, and the film goes up there and stays. Among the children is Verónico, whose mother died and whose father left to look for work when the boy was an infant, a fact stated early and never worked up into pathos. Miguel Pereira built the picture from Fortunato Ramos's account of his own years teaching in the region, and the borrowing shows less in incident than in patience: the film knows how long a term is from inside a rural school, and what a household gives up to send a child to one. Argentina sent it to the Academy Awards, which is a peculiar journey for a film so intent on staying put. In that hamlet, for a long way in any direction, the classroom is the largest institution in sight.

Yuichi draws manga, writes songs, keeps a salaryman's desk, and looks in on his mother, whose memory has been going since his father died. Mitsue is funny and exhausting in about equal measure, and the question in the house is whether she should be moved somewhere with staff, a decision Yuichi and his own son are being asked to make soon. Then the film steps back decades and hands her to a younger actress: one of ten children, a war to survive, a drinking husband to keep upright. Azuma Morisaki was the oldest working director in Japan when he shot it, and that arithmetic is doing something. Broad comedy carries the whole load, drawn thick and played for laughs, without softening the plain fact that remembering has become a job somebody else in the family has to do.

A diamond goes on display in seven days, and that is the entire clock this thing runs on. Lupin has already emptied the race track for whatever it was worth; the complication is a girl he pulls out of a crowd of thugs, whose father turns out to be rich and attached to the stone. What follows is less a heist than a labor market. An old mercenary is sent to talk Jigen into changing sides, Goemon is already working for Fujiko, and the crew Lupin counts on keeps taking calls from people who can pay. Hajime Kamegaki has ninety minutes and a television slot, so nothing gets explained: the thieves arrive fully formed, the double-crosses land on schedule, and the plan is assembled while it is already being carried out.

The department is cosmetics, the product is deodorant, and the job is to find out what teenagers think of a new cream for pimples. Roland Jung wanted to write. What a person wants has less standing than the rent, so he takes the agency work in Stockholm and is handed a brief. Bo Widerberg plays the machinery straight enough to become absurd: the survey is designed, the young are consulted about their skin with the gravity of a public inquiry, the findings are written up and delivered. The comedy is not that advertising is foolish but that it is thorough, that a man with something of his own to write can be fully occupied, and reasonably paid, by the question of whether adolescents will buy a tube of anything.

Adapting a poem is a different job from adapting a story: the events transfer easily and the voice is what resists. Leopoldo Torre Nilsson took José Hernández's Martín Fierro and made a Western of it, a gaucho who will not be governed, the people living alongside him, the Argentine Pampas going out in every direction. Some of the genre fits without argument, the distance and the horses and a man reached last by whatever authority is in charge. Some of it does not, and the friction is where the film gets interesting, because a frontier picture wants incident and a poem wants cadence, and two hours has to satisfy both. Whatever the verse does on the page, this has to do with faces, silence, and the time it takes to cross open ground.
